# Spine

> Who is well in the clinic, who is labelled ill, and where does infant death still sit on the map?
Both panels together show who in the clinic is labelled ill: how heart disease splits across sex and chest-pain type, and whether high blood sugar and exercise-induced angina go together more than chance would predict.


# Introduction — the tables we own

This folder is ours for the ten days. Three tables, three shapes.

- **Panel A** (`panel-A.csv`) — clinic measurements: age, blood pressure, cholesterol, maximum heart rate, plus sex and heart-disease label for grouping.
- **Panel B** (`panel-B.csv`) — the *same people*, Quals only: chest pain, blood sugar flag, exercise angina, heart disease.
- **Panel C** (`panel-C.csv`) — infant mortality by country. No geometry in the file; we join to a world map in R.

A does not grow a mosaic. B does not grow a honest histogram of chest pain. C is a rate, not a headcount.

We load from this folder:
{{< include _setup.qmd >}}

```{r}
#| label: Set Up Chunk
library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
library(skimr)
library(vcd)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(countrycode)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(leaflet)
library(magrittr)
```

Found tables train the mark. A campus Free Hunch, if we collect one, is a **made** panel of the same pair type — new people, old grammar. It does not replace A, B, or C.


# Panel A — body / measure

*Age, BP, Cholesterol, MaximumHR are Quant. Sex and HeartDisease are Quals used to *split* the Quants.*

```{r}
#| label: My Panel A data
myPanelAData <-  read_csv(file = "data/panel-A.csv")
```


### 1. See the table

What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?

The Qualitative variable in this table entail - HeartDisease and Sex(These were character variables which were mutated to factor variables).

the quantitative variables in this table are - Age, BP, Cholestrol, MaximumHR.

A few piecies of data missing here are the fatality rate and the fact that casuality cannot be proved since this is not an RCT data set.

```r
# glimpse() / inspect() / skim()
```

```{r}
#| label: Table for Panel A
glimpse(myPanelAData)
skim(myPanelAData)
```

```{r}
#| label: change to factor(Panel A)
myPanelAData |> mutate(Sex = as.factor(Sex))
myPanelAData |> mutate(HeartDisease = as.factor(HeartDisease))
myPanelAMod <- myPanelAData |> dplyr::mutate(Sex = as.factor(Sex), HeartDisease = as.factor(HeartDisease))
glimpse(myPanelAMod)
```

### 2. Ask

One question *this* table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Question can answer:

1.How does cholestrol affect different sex?

2.Based on sex and age how does the maximum Heartrate fluctuate?

3.How does the age distribution of people with and without heart disease differ in this dataset?

4.how does the number of men and women having BP vary over the years?

Questions it cannot answer:

1.For what % of the population is cholestrol the reason for heart disease?

2.Does sex itself influence a person's maximum heart rate, or are the differences in maximum heart rate actually related to other factors such as age or health?

### 3. Choose a mark

 Questions can be answered:

```{r}
#| label: Chart1-Question1A
myPanelAData |> gf_boxplot(~ Cholesterol, bins = 50, fill = ~ Sex)
```

```{r}
#| label: Chart2-Question2A
myPanelAData |> gf_point(MaximumHR~Age, color = ~Sex) |>  gf_smooth(method = "lm") |>  gf_density_2d()
```

```{r}
#| label: Chart3-Question3A
myPanelAData |> gf_boxplot(Age ~ HeartDisease)
```

```{r}
#| label: Chart4 - Question4A
myPanelAMod |> gf_line(BP ~ Age,bins= 100, color =  ~Sex)
```

Questions that cannot be answered:
```{r}
#| label: Chart1- Question1AN
myPanelAData |> gf_point(Cholesterol~Sex,color = ~HeartDisease)
```

```{r}
#| label: Chart2-Question2AN
myPanelAData |> ggplot(aes(Sex, MaximumHR, fill = Sex)) + geom_violin(alpha = 0.6) + geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.3, size = 1) + theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: Statistic Test 1- Summarize
myPanelAData |> group_by(Sex) |> summarize( mean_MaximumHR = mean(MaximumHR, na.rm = TRUE))
myPanelAData |> group_by(Sex) |> summarize( mean_Cholesterol = mean(Cholesterol, na.rm = TRUE))
myPanelAData |> group_by(Sex) |> summarize( mean_BP = mean(BP, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r}
#| label: Statistic Test 2- T-Test
mosaic::t_test(MaximumHR ~ Sex, data = myPanelAData)
mosaic::t_test(Cholesterol ~ Sex, data = myPanelAData)
mosaic::t_test(BP ~ Sex, data = myPanelAData)

```

### 4. Predict: What do we think we will see?

We predict that age, sex, blood pressure, and cholesterol will show noticeable differences in maximum heart rate and heart disease.

### 5. Say

Title:
Age and sex show different patterns in heart health measures.

Caption:
The graphs show how age, sex, blood pressure, cholesterol, maximum heart rate, and heart disease are distributed and related across the sample.

One sentence we will stand behind:
The data shows differences between groups, but these patterns do not prove that one factor causes heart disease.

### 6. Limit
What this panel cannot do. Which kit table we refused to abuse.
The data available to us in this panel cannot prove dependency in terms of causality between two or more variables.



# Panel B — category / talk

*ChestPain, Sex, HeartDisease, ExerciseInducedAngina. Mosaic or stacked bar. No mean of ChestPain.*

```{r}
#| label: My Panel B Data
myPanelBData <-  read_csv(file = "data/panel-B.csv")
```

### 1. See the table

What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?

```r
# glimpse() / inspect() / skim()
```
```{r}
#| label: Table for Panel B
myPanelBData <-  read_csv(file = "data/panel-B.csv")
glimpse(myPanelBData)
inspect(myPanelBData)
skim(myPanelBData)
```

```{r}
#| label: Change to factor(Panel B)
myPanelBData |> mutate(Sex = as.factor(Sex))
myPanelBData |> mutate(HeartDisease = as.factor(HeartDisease))
myPanelBData |> mutate(ChestPain = as.factor(ChestPain))
myPanelBData |> mutate(ExerciseInducedAngina = as.factor(ExerciseInducedAngina))
myPanelBMod <- myPanelBData |> dplyr::mutate(Sex = as.factor(Sex), HeartDisease = as.factor(HeartDisease), ChestPain = as.factor(ChestPain), ExerciseInducedAngina = as.factor(ExerciseInducedAngina))
glimpse(myPanelBMod)

```

### 2. Ask

Questions that can be answered:

1. What part of the population posses both Blood Sugar and Heart Diseases?

2. How does the proportion of people with HeartDisease vary across different types of chest pain?

3. How does the distribution of Exercise Induced Angina differ between males and females? 

Questions that cannot be answered:

 1. How often does Exercise Induced Angina cause Chest Pain amongst men and women?
  
 2. Why do certain types of Chest Pain have higher rates of Heart Disease?
 
 3. What factors are responsible for certain people having heart diseases?
 
### 3. Choose a mark
Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

Questions that can be answered:
```{r}
#| label: Chart1-Question 1B

myPanelBData |> ggplot(aes(x = BloodSugar, fill = HeartDisease)) +geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Blood Sugar", y = "Number of People")
```

```{r}
#| label: Chart2-Question2B
myPanelBData |> ggplot(aes(x = ChestPain, fill = HeartDisease)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") +labs(title = "Heart Disease Proportion Across Chest Pain Types",x = "Chest Pain Type",y = "Proportion",fill = "Heart Disease") + theme_classic()

```

```{r}
#| label: Chart3-Question3B
myPanelBData |> ggplot(aes(x = ExerciseInducedAngina, fill = HeartDisease)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge") +facet_wrap(~Sex) +
  labs(x = "Exercise-Induced Angina", y = "Number of People")
```

Questions that cannot be answered:
```{r}
#| label: Chart1-Question1BN
vcd::structable(ChestPain ~ ExerciseInducedAngina + Sex, data = myPanelBData) |> vcd::mosaic(labeling = labeling_values(), shade = TRUE, type = "expected")

```

```{r}
#| label: Chart2-Question 2BN
myPanelBData |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = ChestPain, fill = HeartDisease)) + geom_bar() + coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Chest Pain", y = "Number of People")
```

```{r}
#| label: Chart3-Question3BN
vcd::structable(ExerciseInducedAngina ~ BloodSugar, data = myPanelBData) |> vcd::mosaic(labeling = labeling_values, shade = TRUE,gp = shading_Friendly, type = "expected")
```

Statistic
```{r}
#| label: Chi-Square Test
mosaic::xchisq.test(BloodSugar ~ ExerciseInducedAngina, data = myPanelBData)
mosaic::xchisq.test(ChestPain ~ ExerciseInducedAngina, data = myPanelBData)
```

Observations and Conclusions Drawn:

Blood Sugar ~ Exercise Induced Angina-
The above test proves that there is no significant correlation between the two variables. It states that the Blood Sugar and Exercise Induced Angina are independent of each other.
Further since the p value exceeds 0.5 it fails to prove the fact that nothing is happening.

Chest Pain ~ Exercise Induced Angina-
The above test proves that there is strong association between the two variables. Chest Pain and Exercise Induced Angina are Highly dependent on each other.
The low p value proves the hypothesis that nothing is happening. 

### 4. Predict: What do we think we will see?

We predict that heart disease will be more common among people with certain chest pain types, exercise-induced angina, and high blood sugar.

### 5. Say

Title:
Heart disease shows different patterns across several health-related factors.

Caption:
The graphs compare heart disease with chest pain, blood sugar, exercise-induced angina, and sex to identify patterns within the sample.

One sentence we will stand behind:
The data shows associations between heart disease and these factors, but it cannot tell us what causes heart disease.


### 6. Limit

What this panel cannot do:
This panel can show associations between the variables, but it cannot explain why these patterns occur or prove that one factor causes heart disease.

Which kit table we refused to abuse:
The contingency table.


# Panel C — place

*Join `country` to `rnaturalearth` / `tmap::World`. Fill is infant mortality (a rate).*
```{r}
#| label: My Panel C Data
myPanelCData <-  read_csv(file = "data/panel-C.csv")
```


### 1. See the table

What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?

The quantitative variable in this dataset is - Infant mortality Rate

The qualitative variable in this dataset is - The country name 

Geometry as a Multipolygon was added after merging the world selected dataset.

A few variables that are missing are time line, gender, age of death, etc.


```{r}
#| label: Table for Panel C

glimpse(myPanelCData)
inspect(myPanelCData)
skim(myPanelCData)
```

```{r}
world <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(returnclass = "sf")
glimpse(world)
world |> ggformula::gf_sf(geometry = ~geometry)
world_selected <- world |> dplyr::select(name, geometry)
glimpse(world_selected)
```


```{r}
#| label: Finding Missing Countries
missing_countries <- setdiff(unique(myPanelCData$country), unique(world_selected$name))
print(missing_countries)
length(missing_countries)
```


```{r}
#| label: Cleaning Spatial Dataset

world_hires    <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")
world_selected <- world_hires |> dplyr::select(name, iso_a3_eh, geometry)

```


```{r}
#| label: Merging Datasets Together
panelC_fixed <- myPanelCData |>
  dplyr::filter(country != "European Union") |>   # not a country, so no polygon exists
  dplyr::mutate(
    
    iso3 = countrycode::countrycode(country, origin = "country.name", destination = "iso3c",
             custom_match = c("FaroeIslands"            = "FRO",
                              "NorthernMariana Islands" = "MNP",
                              "Virgin Islands"          = "VIR")),
    
    country = dplyr::case_match(country,
      "United States"                     ~ "United States of America",
      "Congo, Democratic Republic of the" ~ "Dem. Rep. Congo",
      "Congo, Republic of the"            ~ "Congo",
      "Central African Republic"          ~ "Central African Rep.",
      "Equatorial Guinea"                 ~ "Eq. Guinea",
      "South Sudan"                       ~ "S. Sudan",
      "Gambia, The"                       ~ "Gambia",
      "Cote d'Ivoire"                     ~ "C\u00f4te d'Ivoire",
      "Swaziland"                         ~ "eSwatini",
      "Western Sahara"                    ~ "W. Sahara",
      "Burma"                             ~ "Myanmar",
      "Korea, North"                      ~ "North Korea",
      "Korea, South"                      ~ "South Korea",
      "Dominican Republic"                ~ "Dominican Rep.",
      "Solomon Islands"                   ~ "Solomon Is.",
      "Bahamas, The"                      ~ "Bahamas",
      "Bosnia and Herzegovina"            ~ "Bosnia and Herz.",
      "Macedonia"                         ~ "North Macedonia",
      "Czech Republic"                    ~ "Czechia",
      "West Bank"                         ~ "Palestine",   # the map has one polygon for both
      "Gaza Strip"                        ~ "Palestine",
      .default = country)
  ) |>

  dplyr::group_by(country, iso3) |>
  dplyr::summarise(inf_mort_rate = mean(inf_mort_rate), .groups = "drop")


myPanelCMod <- world_selected |>
  dplyr::left_join(panelC_fixed |> dplyr::select(country, rate_name = inf_mort_rate),
                   by = c("name" = "country")) |>
  dplyr::left_join(panelC_fixed |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(iso3)) |> dplyr::select(iso3, rate_iso = inf_mort_rate),
                   by = c("iso_a3_eh" = "iso3")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(inf_mort_rate = dplyr::coalesce(rate_name, rate_iso)) |>
  dplyr::select(name, iso_a3_eh, inf_mort_rate, geometry)

glimpse(myPanelCMod)
```

### 2. Ask

Questions that can be answered:

1.Which continent has the countries with maximum infant mortality rate?

2. What is the distribution of infant mortality rate across the European countries?

Questions that cannot be answered:

1. How has the infant mortality rate changed over time across genders?

2. How does the infant mortality rate differ across a country through its different parts- urban/ rural?


### 3. Choose a mark
Geom, map mark, or (later) test that matches the pair type. Name it before you code.

Questions that can be answered:

```{r}
#| label: Chart 1- Question1A
still_missing <- panelC_fixed |>
  dplyr::filter(!(country %in% world_selected$name), !(iso3 %in% world_selected$iso_a3_eh))
print(still_missing$country)

myPanelCMod |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::filter(is.na(inf_mort_rate)) |> dplyr::pull(name)
myPanelCMod |> gf_sf(geometry = ~geometry, fill = ~inf_mort_rate)
```

```{r}
#| label: Chart 2 - Question2A
myPanelCData |> filter(countrycode(country, origin= "country.name", destination = "continent" )== "Europe") |>  gf_histogram(~inf_mort_rate, fill =  ~country, bins = 100)
```

Questions that cannot be answered:
```{r}
#| label: Chart 1- Question 1AN
myPanelCData |>filter(country=="Canada") |> gf_boxplot(~inf_mort_rate)
```

```{r}
#| label: Chart 2- Question 2AN
myPanelCMod |> sf::st_centroid() |> dplyr::mutate(lon = sf::st_coordinates(geometry)[,1], lat = sf::st_coordinates(geometry)[,2]) |> gf_point(lat ~ lon, color = ~inf_mort_rate) |> gf_density_2d()

```


### 4. Predict
We expected to see geographical disparity in increased infant mortality rates, however the obtained density chart portayed similar levels of infant mortality rates within close proximity.

### 5. Say
Title:
Infant mortality rates vary vastly across countries

Caption:
The graphs help understand infant mortality rates accross different countries, however it is not possible to zoom into regions within these countries.

One sentence we will stand behind:
The data correlates the names of countries to their geometry, while using a colour gradient to portray infant mortality rate.

The continent of Africa has the highest mortality rate, however what astonishes me is the fact that the data provided can only point to so much - one cannot zoom in to see what locality has higher infant mortality rate nor see the development over time.


### 6. Limit

This panel cannot prove causality, nor does it allow us to plot bar graphs or histograms without over complicating understanding- the data set is limited to 1 qual and 1 quan variable to which geometry has been associated.


# Conclusion

Across our three panels, we explored patterns in health, categorical variables, and differences between countries. We used boxplots, bar charts, scatterplots,and density maps to understand how variables relate to one another.

- The question we will defend in ninety seconds
How can data visualisation help us identify patterns without assuming that one variable causes another? Further how can we be expected to plot graphs without necessary data?

- What we will **not** claim
We will not claim that association proves causation, however in a human mind identifying patterns often associates one factor to be the cause of another, hence our graphs only portray patterns that a human mind can pick up on - they in no was display factual correlation.

- Which lines were human, which were machine
We chose the questions and interpreted the patterns as a group, while R and its packages helped us create graphs, conduct statistical tests, and present the data. The tools helped with the process, but interpreting the results required our own judgement. Further even while coding if we used AI to generate a code- after using it to understand what needs to be done, we simplified the code to functions we had learned and coded it ourselves.

HOWEVER THE COUNTRY CODE PART OF PANEL C IS PARTIALLY AI GENERATED

- Limits: sample, missingness, the test we did not run
Our conclusions are limited by the available variable, missing data for a particular year or country cannot be plotted by us, further any data required to prove causality or any data used while merging 2 data frames is sensitive to deal with and requires caution.


- Gift for the steal-this strip (palette, annotation, join trick)
Creating a uniform theme for fonts and colours helped with consistency, we realised that data was much easier to follow and read . 

Overall, we learned that a good graph is not just about appearance. It should answer a meaningful question, represent the data honestly, and make its limitations clear. Further we also learned how we need to pay attention to details like syntax and spellings while being daring enough to experiment with different codes.




## Panel D - Erin Brokovich - Interactive Data Map


```{r}
plume <- tibble(
    lng = c(-117.165, -117.157, -117.165, -117.178, -117.190,
            -117.205, -117.218, -117.222, -117.212, -117.198,
            -117.182, -117.172),
    lat = c(34.900, 34.906, 34.918, 34.932, 34.945,
            34.958, 34.962, 34.952, 34.938, 34.922,
            34.907, 34.898)
)

landmarks <- tibble(
    name = c("PG&E Hinkley Compressor Station", "Hinkley"),
    lat  = c(34.9030, 34.95),
    lng  = c(-117.1612, -117.2)
)
```


Chromium Concentration For Each Home

```{r}
hinkley_homes <- tibble(
    name = c("Jensen Family", "Robinson Family",
             "Family 1(Hypothetical)", "Family 2(Hypothetical)"),
    pop  = c(3, 2, 4, 5),
    lat  = c(34.9512, 34.9514, 34.9480, 34.9440),
    lng  = c(-117.2051, -117.2046, -117.2030, -117.2090),
    cr6_ppb = c(3.14, 2.85, 1.20, 0.45) 
)

hinkley_symptoms <- tibble(
    name = c("Jensen Family", "Jensen Family", "Jensen Family",
             "Robinson Family", "Robinson Family",
             "Family 1(Hypothetical)", "Family 1(Hypothetical)",
             " Family 2(Hypothetical)", "Family 2(Hypothetical)"),
    symptom = c("Tumors", "Hysterectomy", "Hodgkin's disease",
                "Breast cancer", "Miscarriages",
                "Nosebleeds", "Skin rashes",
                "Chronic pain", "Ulcers")
)
```

Merging Symptoms into hinkley_homes

```{r}
hinkley_homes <- hinkley_homes |> 
    left_join(
        hinkley_symptoms |> 
            group_by(name) |> 
            summarise(symptoms = paste(symptom, collapse = ", ")),
        by = "name"
    )
```

Adding Font & Colour

```{r}
custom_font   <- "Times New Roman, sans-serif" 
text_color    <- "#6a5acd"           
bg_color      <- "#e6e6fa"           
border_color  <- "#8a2be2"          

leaflet() |> 
    addTiles() |> 
    setView(lng = -117.2, lat = 34.95, zoom = 12) |> 
    addPolygons(data = plume, lng = ~lng, lat = ~lat,
                color = "darkgreen", weight = 2, fillOpacity = 0.4, fillColor = "lightgreen") |> 
    addMarkers(data = landmarks, popup = ~name) |> 
    addCircles(data = hinkley_homes, radius = 150,
               color = "lightblue", fillColor = "purple", fillOpacity = 0.3) |> 
    addCircleMarkers(
        data = hinkley_homes,
        radius = ~pop * 3,
        color = "darkgreen",
        fillColor = ~ifelse(cr6_ppb > 2.0, "lightgreen", "lightblue"), # Color-code based on Cr-6 level
        stroke = TRUE,
        weight = 1,
        fillOpacity = 0.8,
        label = ~paste0(
            "<div style='font-family: ", custom_font, "; ",
            "color: ", text_color, "; ",
            "background-color: ", bg_color, "; ",
            "border: 1px solid ", border_color, "; ",
            "padding: 6px; border-radius: 4px;'>",
            "<b>", name, "</b><br/>",
            "Population: ", pop, "<br/>",
            "<b>Chromium-6:</b> ", cr6_ppb, " ppb<br/>",
            "<b>Symptoms:</b> ", symptoms,
            "</div>"
        ) %>% lapply(htmltools::HTML),
        labelOptions = labelOptions(
            noHide = TRUE,
            direction = "top",
            style = list("box-shadow" = "2px 2px rgba(0,0,0,0.2)")
        )
    )
```
This Chart Represents the families affected by the Chromium- 6 that Erin spoke to during the course of the film - it puts forth the symptoms displayed by the families as well as the amounts of Chromium ingested.
